context_component: Supportive psychotherapy with structured preparation, facilitator support during dosing, and post-session follow-up
population_or_setting: Adults with moderate or severe major depressive disorder at a specialized research center in Baltimore, Maryland; randomized waiting-list-controlled trial
sample_size: 24 completed the intervention and post-session assessments (13 immediate treatment; 11 delayed treatment); 27 randomized
study_design: Randomized waiting-list-controlled clinical trial; immediate treatment compared with an 8-week delayed-treatment condition
delivery_format: At least 18 in-person visits over 8 weeks; two daylong sessions with two facilitators present during dosing. Participants were prepared in meetings with the facilitators, and received follow-up meetings after dosing. During sessions, music, eyeshades, and headphones were used, with facilitators encouraging inward attention.
relationship_to_outcome_or_safety: Depression improved after the multicomponent psilocybin-assisted therapy intervention compared with the delayed-treatment period. The study did not isolate the contribution of psychotherapy, facilitator support, preparation, follow-up, or the session environment.
dose_or_session_context: Two psilocybin sessions: 20 mg/70 kg in session 1 and 30 mg/70 kg in session 2, approximately 1.6 weeks apart; approximately 11 hours of supportive psychotherapy overall, including 8 hours of preparation and 2–3 hours of follow-up meetings.
timepoint_or_phase: Preparation before session 1; support during both dosing sessions; follow-up after sessions; outcomes assessed at weeks 1 and 4 after session 2
finding_summary: The psilocybin-assisted therapy package, delivered with structured preparation, facilitator support, and follow-up, was associated with lower depression scores than the waiting-list condition at the corresponding assessments. In the immediate-treatment group, mean GRID-HAMD scores were 8.0 and 8.5 at weeks 1 and 4 after session 2, versus 23.8 and 23.5 at weeks 5 and 8 in the delayed-treatment group before treatment. The study does not establish effects of any individual context component.
effect_or_statistic: Between-group Cohen d = 2.5 at week 5 (95% CI, 1.4–3.5; P < .001) and d = 2.6 at week 8 (95% CI, 1.5–3.7; P < .001); time-by-condition interaction ηp² = 0.57 (90% CI, 0.38–0.66; P < .001).

population_or_setting: Adults with chronic PTSD and inadequate response to prior pharmacotherapy and/or psychotherapy; civilians, veterans, and first responders at four clinical sites
sample_size: 63 randomized (active MDMA n=47; control MDMA n=16); primary-endpoint PSQI analyses included active n=45 and control n=16
study_design: Pooled secondary analysis of four randomized, double-blind Phase 2 trials; control 0–40 mg versus active 75–125 mg MDMA during psychotherapy
delivery_format: Individual all-day sessions with a co-therapy team; designated comfortable room, optional eyeshades/headphones, overnight site stay, trained night attendant, and nondrug integration sessions
relationship_to_outcome_or_safety: The psychotherapy context accompanied greater improvement in self-reported sleep quality with active MDMA than control at the primary endpoint; sleep improvement also tracked with PTSD symptom improvement. The pooled analysis does not isolate the contribution of individual psychotherapy components.
dose_or_session_context: Three 90-minute preparatory sessions without drug; two blinded 8-hour experimental sessions 3–5 weeks apart, each followed by three 90-minute integration sessions; active MDMA 75–125 mg or control 0–40 mg, with optional supplemental half-dose
timepoint_or_phase: Preparation and integration surrounding blinded experimental sessions; primary endpoint 1–2 months after blinded sessions, treatment exit, and 12-month follow-up
finding_summary: In the context of manualized MDMA-assisted psychotherapy, active-dose participants had a larger mean PSQI improvement at the primary endpoint than control participants (change −3.53 versus +0.56; p=.003). A drop of at least 3 PSQI points occurred in 53.2% of active-dose participants versus 12.5% of controls (p=.003). Since all participants later received active MDMA, pooled follow-up analyses showed PSQI improvement from baseline at treatment exit and 12 months (both p<.001), with further improvement from treatment exit to 12 months (p=.030). Change in PSQI and CAPS-IV from baseline to treatment exit was correlated (r=.371, p=.004).
effect_or_statistic: Primary endpoint PSQI change: active M=−3.53, SD=5.03; control M=0.56, SD=3.05; p=.003; Hedges' g=0.88. At least 3-point PSQI reduction: 53.2% versus 12.5%, p=.003. Follow-up PSQI: baseline-to-treatment exit and baseline-to-12-month p<.001; treatment exit-to-12-month p=.030. Baseline-to-treatment-exit change correlation with CAPS-IV: r=.371, p=.004.

study_title: Modifying Informed Consent to Help Address Functional Unmasking in Psychedelic Clinical Trials
abstract: IMPORTANCE: There is unprecedented clinician, industry, and patient interest in the therapeutic development of psychedelic drugs. This is due to a combination of promising clinical trial results, positive media coverage, and the lack of novel pharmacologic treatments for psychiatric disorders in recent decades. However, the field faces a key methodological challenge: masking participants to treatment conditions in psychedelic clinical trials has been largely unsuccessful. OBJECTIVE: When participants can tell whether they received active drug or placebo, their responses to clinical assessments, questionnaires, and even their functional imaging and biological data can be influenced by preconceptions about treatment effects. Positive patient expectancies combined with ineffective masking may skew outcomes and inflate effect sizes. This complicates efforts to determine the safety and efficacy of psychedelic drugs. Here, we explore a method to help address this problem: modifying informed consent to obscure information about the study design. EVIDENCE REVIEW: We reviewed all contemporary (2000-2024) clinical trials of psychedelic or methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) therapy and corresponded with the investigators to compile information on the use of modifications to informed consent in these studies. FINDINGS: Modifying informed consent to obscure details of the study design has been implemented in several psychedelic clinical trials and may offer a way to strengthen masking. However, this approach poses significant ethical risks. We examine examples of modifications used in the psychedelic literature, discuss the current regulatory landscape, and suggest strategies to mitigate risks associated with modified informed consent. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Incorporating modified informed consent in future psychedelic clinical trials may improve interpretability and impact, but this has not been explicitly tested. Modifications to informed consent may not be appropriate in all cases, and risks to participants should be minimized by implementing appropriate guardrails.
finding_summary: The review recommends safeguards for psychedelic trials that modify consent, including debriefing, consideration of participant-authorized modifications and community input, measurement of expectancy and masking success, and publication of consent language.

study_title: Is the Requirement for First-Person Experience of Psychedelic Drugs a Justified Component of a Psychedelic Therapist’s Training?
abstract: Recent research offers good reason to think that various psychedelic drugs-including psilocybin, ayahuasca, ketamine, MDMA, and LSD-may have significant therapeutic potential in the treatment of various mental health conditions, including post-traumatic stress disorder, depression, existential distress, and addiction. Although the use of psychoactive drugs, such as Diazepam or Ritalin, is well established, psychedelics arguably represent a therapeutic step change. As experiential therapies, their value would seem to lie in the subjective experiences they induce. As it is the only way for trainee psychedelic therapists to fully understand their subjective effects, some have suggested that firsthand experience of psychedelics should form part of training programs. We question this notion. First, we consider whether the epistemic benefits offered by drug-induced psychedelic experience are as unique as is supposed. We then reflect on the value it might have in regard to the training of psychedelic therapists. We conclude that, absent stronger evidence of the contribution drug-induced experiences make to the training of psychedelic therapists, requiring trainees to take psychedelic drugs does not seem ethically legitimate. However, given the potential for epistemic benefit cannot be entirely ruled out, permitting trainees who wish to gain first-hand experience of psychedelics may be permissible.
finding_summary: Patients may differ in whether they prefer a therapist who has personally experienced psychedelics, so patient preferences do not support making that experience a universal training requirement.
support: Patients may differ in whether they prefer a therapist who has personally experienced psychedelics, so patient preferences do not support making that experience a universal training requirement.
notes: The paper mentions some evidence that patients consider therapist experience somewhat important, but does not provide details or establish a uniform preference.
supporting_quote: it is unlikely that all those who might be offered psychedelic therapy will have a uniform position on this matter | That patients will likely take different perspectives on the matter provides further reason to create training routes that do not require therapists to take psychedelics.

bundle_summary: The review argues that first-person psychedelic experience may offer trainee therapists some insight into profound affective states, but does not ensure understanding of patients and is not the only possible source of relevant insight. Given the absence of strong evidence that it improves training, requiring psychedelic use is ethically unjustified; voluntary choice is preferable, particularly in light of possible contraindications and varied patient preferences.
